summary: This document describes JSON data structures that represent registration information held by Regional Internet Registries and Domain Name Registries. They form the responses of RDAP queries. It obsoletes RFC 7483.

eli5.summary: When you look up who owns a website, the answer arrives as a tidy list. This document defines the layout of that answer so every program can read it.

questions: what does an rdap response look like
subtitle: The JSON shapes that registries use to answer 'who holds this domain, IP block or AS number?'

tldr.problem: Registries answer lookups about domains, IP address blocks and AS numbers, and clients need those answers in one predictable, machine-readable format.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9083 defines JSON data types, shared structures (links, notices, events, status) and five object classes (entity, nameserver, domain, IP network, autnum), plus formats for errors, help, searches and truncated results.
tldr.outcome: It is an Internet Standard (STD 95) that obsoletes RFC 7483, so it is the current definition of RDAP response bodies.

today: RFC 9083 is an Internet Standard (STD 95) and no later RFC obsoletes it. It obsoletes RFC 7483, which defined the earlier version of these JSON responses.

sections.title: What RDAP Responses Describe
sections.content:
The Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP) answers queries about registration data held by Regional Internet Registries (RIRs) and Domain Name Registries (DNRs). RFC 9082 defines the queries and RFC 7480 describes how they travel over HTTP. RFC 9083 defines the JSON answers.

The data model has five parts: simple data types, reusable data structures, object classes for a lookup of one object, arrays of objects for a search, and the error response. A lookup of a single object returns one JSON object. A search returns a JSON object that holds an array of results.

RIRs and DNRs overlap a lot, so the document gives one unified model for both. Domains, nameservers and entities are returned by both kinds of registry. RIRs additionally serve IP networks and Autonomous System numbers.
sections.eli5: Many offices keep lists of who owns what. This document is the standard form they all fill in when someone asks, so the answers look the same everywhere.

sections.title: Using JSON: Naming and Extensions
sections.content:
Clients SHOULD ignore JSON members they do not recognise. A server may add members that the RFC does not define, and that is not an error. Servers that do so SHOULD prefix the member name with a short identifier and an underscore. The RFC's fictional Registry of the Moon uses lunarNIC, giving names such as lunarNIC_beforeOneSmallStep.

Clients must also expect any optional member to be missing, because servers may omit unrequired members according to their own policies. All JSON names in the document are case sensitive, and both sides MUST send and process them in the specified case.

Extensions are announced through the rdapConformance array. The literal rdap_level_0 means conformance with this specification. A custom extension must add its own unique string registered in the IANA RDAP Extensions registry from RFC 7480.
sections.eli5: You may add your own extra boxes to the form, as long as you put your club name in front of them. People who do not know your boxes simply skip them.

sections.title: Common Data Types
sections.content:
The RFC fixes how a few kinds of value are written as JSON strings. A handle is a registry-unique identifier for an object. IPv4 addresses use dotted-decimal notation and IPv6 addresses follow the forms in RFC 5952. Country codes use the two-character alpha-2 designation from ISO 3166. Dates and times follow RFC 3339 and URIs follow RFC 3986.

DNS names come in two forms. LDH names use only letters, digits and hyphens. Unicode names contain at least one U-label. Trailing periods are optional in both.

Contact information uses jCard, the JSON form of vCard. Its fn member is required and must not be null, but an empty fn may be used when the contact name does not exist or is redacted.
sections.eli5: The form says how to write things: dates one way, country codes as two letters, web names with or without fancy letters. That way nobody has to guess.

sections.title: Common Data Structures
sections.content:
Several small structures are reused inside every object class.

  • rdapConformance: an array of strings naming the specifications used. It MUST appear in the topmost object of a response and nowhere else.
  • links: objects with value, rel and href (all required) and optional hreflang, title, media and type. A related link must not have the same href as the self link, to avoid infinite client loops.
  • notices and remarks: arrays of objects with a required description array and optional title, type and links. Notices describe the service or whole response and appear only in the topmost object. Remarks describe the object that contains them.
  • lang: a language identifier for the data.
  • events: each has a required eventAction and eventDate, an optional eventActor and optional links. Events can be future dated, for example to show when an object expires.
  • status, port43 (the WHOIS server for the object), publicIds and objectClassName. The objectClassName is required in every RDAP response object.
sections.eli5: Every record has the same small building blocks: web links, notes, a history of what happened and when, and a label saying what kind of thing it is.

sections.title: The Five Object Classes
sections.content:
Each object class carries a links array. Servers SHOULD include a self link with type application/rdap+json so clients can cache the object, but clients MUST cope when it is missing. Clients SHOULD NOT cache an object whose self link has a different authority than the server that returned it, which guards against cache poisoning.

  • Entity: people, organizations, governments, clubs and informal groups, all modelled with one construct. Contact details use jCard. A roles array gives the entity's relationship to the object that contains it, and entities can nest.
  • Nameserver: a DNS nameserver, with ldhName, unicodeName and an ipAddresses object holding v4 and v6 arrays. Some registries treat nameservers as first-class objects and others only as an attribute of a domain, so the class allows both.
  • Domain: a DNS name and point of delegation, with nameservers, entities, IDN variants and a secureDNS object for DNSSEC data such as zoneSigned, delegationSigned, dsData and keyData.
  • IP network: RIR only. It has startAddress, endAddress, ipVersion (v4 or v6), name, type, country and parentHandle.
  • Autnum: RIR only. It has startAutnum and endAutnum, each an unsigned 32-bit integer, plus name, type and country.
sections.eli5: There are five kinds of record: a person or group, a computer that answers name questions, a website name, a block of internet addresses, and a network number. Each has its own set of boxes.

sections.title: Errors, Help, Searches and Truncation
sections.content:
A non-answer response may carry a more descriptive body. It contains a required numeric errorCode matching the HTTP status, plus an optional title and an optional description array. A response to a /help query uses the notices structure.

Search responses hold arrays of the matching object class inside the response object. The array names are domainSearchResults, nameserverSearchResults and entitySearchResults.

When data must be limited, the response is called truncated. It is still valid JSON, but some results or some fields are missing. A server may flag this with a typed notice, or with a typed remark when a single object was cut short.
sections.eli5: If something goes wrong, the answer says what and why. If there are too many results, the answer can say 'I cut this short' so you know it is not the whole list.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
Because JSON is a subset of JavaScript, implementers are advised to follow Section 12 of RFC 8259 to prevent code injection, and to heed the security considerations in RFC 7480 and RFC 7481.

RDAP can return DNSSEC key data, but the parent zone's signature is not carried with it. Those keys are therefore disconnected from their chain of trust and are not generally expected to be trusted without additional information, even though the HTTPS channel protects the connection. Caching clients should guard against cache poisoning.

For privacy, the RFC suggests three status values: private (not shared unless the user is authorized), removed (collected but omitted from the response) and obscured (value altered so it is not easily discernible). Servers MUST support UTF-8 as the default text encoding.
sections.eli5: Some details are secret. The answer can say 'this part is hidden', 'removed' or 'scrambled' so private information stays private.
